evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.text: The database describes 頁 in oracle and bronze forms as 卩 plus 首: a kneeling human figure with the head visually prominent. It says the graph denotes ‘head’; 頁 and 首 differ in whether the body is drawn and are graphic variants. Its examples include oracle-bone uses meaning ‘pig’s head’ (合集15684) and ‘bowing the head’ (合集22215); it notes a Western Zhou bronze occurrence in 卯簋蓋 and a phrase 頁手 there, possibly abbreviated or erroneous. It reports that 頁 and 首 were originally one graph pronounced like 首, and that 頁 had acquired the reading 胡結切 by the Eastern Han at the latest. The source calls the paper measure use a俗字 for 葉. Its account of shape change says oracle-bone 頁 may show or omit hair; a W. Zhou bronze has hair; Warring States forms often distort the hair as 止; the small-seal form omits it. This is a database’s paleographic analysis, not direct visual inspection in this research.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.field: 說文解字；音韻方言；字源字形
evidence.text: The page reproduces the Shuowen entry 頁, ‘head’, analyzed as from 𦣻 and 儿, and gives 胡結切. It also reproduces Duan Yucai’s note disputing the received wording and explaining the entry as an old form associated with 䭬/首; this records a later textual-critical interpretation, not a settled ancient graphic analysis. The page lists oracle-bone examples (including 乙8780 and 合22217), a mid-Western Zhou bronze 卯簋蓋, Chu bamboo-and-silk examples, a Shuowen small-seal form, and Eastern Han clerical evidence. Its dictionary explains the paper/page use as俗用頁 for 葉 and quotes Qing scholar Zhu Junsheng’s statement that 葉 was the proper graph and 頁 was the common form.
evidence.title: 頁 yè、xié - 漢典

evidence.field: Chinese > Glyph origin; pronunciation; Old Chinese
evidence.text: This opened secondary lexicon reports a pictographic analysis combining 卩 and 首, says 頁 and 首 were originally the same head pictograph with the body included in the 頁 form, and reports 頁 used by Eastern Han as a popular alternative for 葉 with paper-sheet/page meaning. It lists modern Mandarin yè for the page sense and xié for head, and Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese /*leb/ and /*ɡleːd/ under two readings. Treat these as the page’s compiled claims; the CUHK character-specific analysis independently supports the broad distinction between the head graph and paper-use spelling, but not every reconstruction or precise dating claim.

evidence.text: The supplied local Unihan_Readings.txt rows give kMandarin yè for both 頁 (U+9801) and 页 (U+9875). The required official character-specific Unicode lookups were attempted at https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=9801 and ...?codepoint=9875, but neither page was accessible through the browser. Therefore the local rows are recorded as supplied dataset evidence only and cannot be presented as verified external Unicode-page evidence. No phonetic-component claim is made for either graph.

gaps: The official Unicode Unihan lookup pages for U+9801 and U+9875 were attempted but inaccessible; supplied local kMandarin rows are not substituted for verified external click-through evidence.

The proposed adoption of 頁 as a common spelling for 葉 in the page/sheet sense is supported as a lexicographic account, but this research did not independently identify and verify the earliest dated attestation of that borrowed use or a full sequence of dated semantic extensions.

The head reading xié is supported lexicographically and by the cited Guangyun fanqie, while the page-use yè is also recorded; this work did not independently establish the historical sound path behind their separate readings. Do not conflate the page-word borrowing with the graphic origin of the head pictograph.
No claims are made here about a sound component: 頁 is analyzed as a pictographic graph in its head sense, while page/sheet use is a whole-graph borrowing or common-form substitution for 葉.

CUHK reports a possible error/abbreviation in the isolated bronze phrase 頁手; the intended reading is uncertain. Shuowen’s component wording is also text-critically disputed in the reproduced Duan Yucai note.
Glyph images were not visually inspected during this research; graphic descriptions are attributed to the opened database and dictionary analyses.
